source_metadata.exact_title: Oral anticoagulant use and incident dementia in atrial fibrillation by baseline LIBRA score: a population-based cohort study using the 45 and Up Study
source_metadata.source_type: original journal article; population-based prospective cohort study

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether oral anticoagulant use was associated with incident dementia in atrial fibrillation and whether the association varied by baseline LIBRA score and key clinical subgroups.
The investigators conducted a population-based prospective cohort study using the Sax Institute 45 and Up Study linked to administrative health records in New South Wales, Australia.
The 45 and Up Study cohort was linked to prescription, hospital admission, emergency department, mental health, cancer, and mortality datasets.
Record linkage by the Centre for Health Record Linkage used probabilistic linkage with manual review of uncertain matches.
Eligible participants were aged at least 45 years and had a first atrial fibrillation diagnosis between 1 January 2010 and 30 June 2022.

population.label: Eligible participants
inclusion_criteria: First AF diagnosis from 1 January 2010 through 30 June 2022

atoms.canonical_statement: Participants with dementia diagnosed before or at the time of atrial fibrillation diagnosis were excluded.

population.label: Eligible participants
exclusion_criteria: Dementia before or at AF diagnosis

atoms.canonical_statement: Participants were required to have at least one year of follow-up after atrial fibrillation diagnosis.

population.label: Eligible participants
inclusion_criteria: At least one year of follow-up after AF diagnosis

atoms.canonical_statement: Primary OAC exposure was defined using a six-month landmark after atrial fibrillation diagnosis: any OAC initiation within six months classified a participant as an OAC user, and no recorded OAC dispensing classified a participant as a non-user.

concept.text: Any oral anticoagulant use within 6 months after AF diagnosis
No recorded OAC dispensing within 6 months after AF diagnosis

atoms.canonical_statement: OACs included warfarin and the DOACs dabigatran, rivaroxaban, and apixaban; OAC users were further classified by the first OAC initiated.
Outcome follow-up for the primary analysis commenced one year after atrial fibrillation diagnosis; participants developing dementia or dying before that point were excluded.
A sensitivity analysis defined adherent long-term OAC exposure as dispensing coverage for at least 80% of total follow-up and classified predominant OAC type using the same threshold.

concept.text: Long-term OAC dispensing coverage ≥80% of follow-up

atoms.canonical_statement: The baseline LIBRA score was constructed as a weighted composite of 11 modifiable dementia risk components; cognitive stimulation was omitted because data were unavailable.
Baseline LIBRA scores were categorised into low-, medium-, and high-risk tertiles for subgroup analysis.
The primary outcome was incident dementia identified using linked hospital, emergency, mental health, death-registration, and antidementia-medication dispensing records.

outcome.definition: Incident dementia identified from linked hospital, emergency, mental health, death-registration, and antidementia-medication dispensing data.

atoms.canonical_statement: The secondary outcome was dementia-related mortality, defined as dementia listed as an underlying or contributing cause of death.

outcome.definition: Dementia recorded as an underlying or contributing cause of death.

atoms.canonical_statement: The primary confounding-control strategy used propensity-score inverse probability of treatment weighting with stabilised weights targeting the average treatment effect.

The propensity model included age, sex, BMI, smoking, heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease, chronic kidney disease, prior stroke, prior major bleeding, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, and anticholinergics; LIBRA, CHA2DS2-VA, and ORBIT scores were excluded to avoid component duplication and multicollinearity.
Stabilised IPTW weights were trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles, and absolute standardised mean differences below 0.10 were considered adequate balance.
Incident dementia associations were estimated with IPTW-weighted Cox proportional hazards models using robust variance estimators and reported as hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals.

Primary Cox models were further adjusted for dyslipidaemia, malignancy, depression, Parkinson disease, calendar year of AF diagnosis, and baseline cardiovascular medications not included in the propensity model.
The 5-year absolute risk reduction was derived from Kaplan-Meier cumulative dementia incidence and the number needed to treat was calculated as 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction.
Prespecified subgroup analyses examined sex, age below versus at least 75 years, LIBRA tertiles, and ORBIT bleeding-risk categories.

Sensitivity analyses used Fine-Gray competing-risk regression, 1:1 propensity-score matching without replacement using a 0.001-SD logit propensity caliper, and restriction to participants with at least 80% OAC dispensing coverage.
Of 48,092 participants with atrial fibrillation, 21,671 met final cohort criteria after exclusions.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that DOAC therapy was associated with lower incident dementia and dementia-related mortality in people with atrial fibrillation.
The authors concluded that the DOAC association was consistent across baseline LIBRA and ORBIT risk categories and was most pronounced among participants aged at least 75 years.
The authors concluded that warfarin was not associated with a consistent reduction in dementia risk because its higher-risk primary estimate attenuated in sensitivity analyses.
The authors stated that the observational findings should not by themselves prompt changes in clinical practice and should await confirmation from randomised trials.
OAC exposure was based on dispensing records rather than confirmed ingestion, and temporary interruptions, discontinuation, switching, and post-landmark adherence changes could not be fully captured.

Residual confounding could not be excluded despite IPTW, matching, multivariable adjustment, and competing-risk analyses; frailty, renal function, socioeconomic status, baseline cognition, and genetic susceptibility were incompletely captured.
Administrative and dispensing data may have missed milder or undiagnosed dementia, and dementia subtypes could not be reliably distinguished.
LIBRA score, comorbidities, risk scores, and concomitant medications were measured only at baseline, so changes during follow-up were not captured.
The cohort was broadly representative of older adults in New South Wales but may not generalise to younger populations.
INR values and time in therapeutic range were unavailable, limiting interpretation of the warfarin association and the quality of warfarin anticoagulation.

The underlying dataset is restricted by the data custodian and cannot be shared publicly; only data explicitly included in the publication are available for review.
